lessons.title: Movement & Sequence
lessons.description: Learn the most fundamental idea in programming: instructions run one after another, in the exact order you write them.
lessons.learning_objective: Explain sequential execution, and write move() commands in the correct order to produce a specific outcome.
lessons.content:
Programming Explanation

Every program, no matter how advanced, is at its core a list of instructions that a computer carries out one at a time, from top to bottom. This is called sequential execution. The computer never skips ahead, never runs two lines at once, and never reorders anything on its own — it simply does exactly what line 1 says, then exactly what line 2 says, and so on.

This matters because order changes outcome. The exact same set of instructions, arranged differently, can produce a completely different result. Learning to plan a sequence before you run it is the first skill every programmer builds.

Code Examples

Knight Code

move(right)
move(right)
move(up)

Real-World Programming

wake_up()
get_dressed()
eat_breakfast()
go_to_school()

Swap get_dressed() and go_to_school() in that second example and the outcome is absurd — the same is true of move() commands. The computer has no common sense to correct a bad order; it just executes exactly what you wrote.

Game Application

In Knight Code, your knight is a program: it executes your move() commands one at a time, in the order you wrote them, with no assumptions of its own. Every level below is solved by reading the grid, planning the full route in your head first, and then writing that route down as a precise sequence.

lessons.title: Making Decisions with If
lessons.description: Teach the knight to check a direction before moving. Learn how an if statement decides whether an instruction should run.
lessons.learning_objective: Explain a condition as a yes-or-no question and use if can(direction) to move only when that direction is possible.
lessons.content:
Your puzzle-room goal

Your challenge is to guide the knight through a puzzle room to its exit. Use an if statement when your route needs a check. The short example below shows one part of a solution, not an entire level.

1. Sometimes we check first

In Lesson 1, the knight followed your instructions in order. But what if there is a wall in the way?

Think about leaving home: if it is raining, take an umbrella. You check something before deciding what to do. Programs can make this kind of decision too.

The question we check is called a condition. Its answer is either true (yes) or false (no).

2. Ask the knight a question

can(right) asks: “Can the knight move right from here?”

  • If movement is possible, the answer is true.
  • If movement is blocked, the answer is false.

Asking the question does not move the knight. We still need a movement instruction.

Try reading this KnightCode program

if can(right):
    move(right)

3. Read it in plain words

“If the knight can move right, move right.”

  1. if tells the program to make a decision.
  2. can(right) is the question it checks.
  3. The colon : starts the instructions for that decision.
  4. The spaces before move(right) show that it belongs to the if statement.

If the answer is false, the program skips that indented move. It does not choose another direction for you.

Use four spaces before the movement line. Type only the code into the terminal.

4. Predict before you run

Imagine the knight has an open path on its right. What will those two lines do? Now imagine a wall blocks its right. What changes?

You can ask about other directions too: can(up), can(down), and can(left).

Your turn: write a program that moves up only if moving up is possible. The programming idea is the same even though the direction changes.

Practice in levels 4–6

  • Check Before Moving: use your first if statement on an open path.
  • What If It Is Blocked?: predict why an indented move is skipped at a wall.
  • You Choose the Condition: choose the right question for each part of a short route.

Check your understanding

If the knight cannot move right, does this program move left instead?

No. It skips move(right). We have not written an instruction to move left.

Why is move(right) indented?

The spaces show that it runs only when the if condition is true.

What is the answer to “Can I move up?” called when movement is possible?

True — another way of saying yes.

lessons.title: Choosing Between Two Actions
lessons.description: Use if and else to tell the knight what to do when a condition is true and what to do when it is false.
lessons.learning_objective: Explain how if/else chooses one of two actions, and predict which action runs for an open or blocked path.
lessons.content:
Your puzzle-room goal

The exit is across the room, and obstacles can put a choice in your route. Use if and else at that choice, then continue toward the exit. A direction being open does not necessarily mean it leads to the goal.

1. Give the program another choice

Our first if statement could choose to move or skip a move. Now let’s give it an alternative.

If it is raining, take an umbrella. Otherwise, leave the umbrella at home. In a program, else means otherwise.

2. Choose a direction

Imagine a junction where the path above the knight is open. We want to go right if we can; otherwise, we will go up.

Try reading this KnightCode program

if can(right):
    move(right)
else:
    move(up)

3. Which instruction runs?

  • Right is open: the condition is true, so the knight moves right. It skips the else part.
  • Right is blocked: the condition is false, so the knight runs the else part and moves up.

Only one of these two choices runs. Notice that else: lines up with if, and each move is indented underneath its own choice.

Important: else does not check whether up is open. We chose up because we already know it is open in this example. An alternative instruction still needs to make sense for the level.

4. Ask the opposite question

blocked(right) asks “Is moving right blocked?” It gives the opposite answer to can(right) at the same position.

On a layout where up is open, this means “If right is blocked, move up.”

Try reading this KnightCode program

if blocked(right):
    move(up)

5. Use evidence, not just appearances

Some wall-looking objects in a level may allow passage. Let can answer whether movement is possible rather than guessing from the picture.

Your turn: suppose up might be blocked but left is open. Write a program that chooses up when possible and left otherwise.

Practice in levels 7–10

  • Right or Up?: make your first two-way choice.
  • When the Answer Is No: use the else part when the first route is blocked.
  • Is It Blocked?: read a condition written with blocked.
  • Looks Can Be Misleading: check whether a wall-looking passage is actually passable.

Check your understanding

Do both moves in the if/else example run?

No. The condition chooses one part, so only that part’s move runs.

Does else automatically find a safe path?

No. It runs the instructions you put under it. You must choose a suitable alternative.

lessons.title: When Actions Change the Situation
lessons.description: Learn why a program sometimes has to do one thing before another. Use buttons, doors, and crates to see those changes happen.
lessons.learning_objective: Explain why opening a door must happen before crossing it, and plan how to keep a pressure plate pressed while the knight moves away.
lessons.content:
Your puzzle-room goal

The exit may be behind a wall that opens. Explore the room, work out which button or plate opens the route, and put those actions into the right order.

1. Do the needed step first

Before you can read a book in a dark room, you might need to turn on the light. Turning it on changes the situation: now you can see.

Programs also need steps in the right order. Doing one action can make a later action possible. In KnightCode, a button can open a door that was blocking the route.

2. Open the way, then check it

Imagine a button one move to the right. After the knight steps on it, the door above that button opens. This program presses the button, then checks the way up.

Try reading this KnightCode program

move(right)
if can(up):
    move(up)

3. Two kinds of switches

  • An ordinary button: once activated, its door stays open when you leave.
  • A pressure plate: its door stays open only while something allowed to press it remains on the plate.

A pressure plate does not use a timer. If you walk away and nothing else holds it down, the door closes.

Before crossing, ask: “Will the door still be open when I reach it?”

4. Let a crate hold the plate

The knight pushes a crate by moving toward it. There is no special push command. The space beyond the crate must be clear.

Some plates accept crates. Leave a crate on one of these plates, and it can hold the door open while the knight walks away. Other switches respond only to the knight, so read the level’s instructions.

Plan in plain words first: push the crate onto the plate → leave it there → take the open route. Then write the movement and condition commands for that plan.

Practice in levels 11–13

  • Open the Way: press an ordinary button before taking its route.
  • Keep It Open: leave a crate on a pressure plate while you continue.
  • Multi-Door Vault, your existing level 13: work out which switch opens each door. Decide what must stay pressed, then solve the room in that order.

Your turn: explain why “stand on the plate, then walk away” may not let you through its door.

Check your understanding

Why should the button step come before the door-crossing step?

The button makes crossing possible by opening the door first.

What can keep a crate-sensitive plate pressed after the knight leaves?

A crate left on the plate.

Why is this a programming lesson?

You are planning how earlier instructions change what later instructions can do.

lessons.title: Repeating Instructions
lessons.description: Use repeat to write an action once and tell the program how many times to do it.
lessons.learning_objective: Use repeat(n) for a known number of repetitions and explain which indented instructions repeat.
lessons.content:
Your puzzle-room goal

Look for a repeated part of the route through the room. A repeat loop handles that part; the rest of your program must still get the knight to the exit.

1. Notice what repeats

Suppose the knight needs to move right three times. You already know how to write that:

Try reading this KnightCode program

move(right)
move(right)
move(right)

2. Write the repetition as a loop

A loop repeats instructions. We can write the same three moves like this:

Try reading this KnightCode program

repeat(3):
    move(right)

3. Read the loop

“Repeat moving right three times.” The number tells the program how many times to repeat. The indented line tells it what to do each time.

The knight still makes three moves. We have written less repeated code; we have not changed the route.

Use repeat when you know the number of repetitions. Check that the moves fit the path: repeat does not check for walls for you.

4. Repeat a small pattern

What if the path goes right, up, right, up? We can repeat a pair of instructions:

Try reading this KnightCode program

repeat(2):
    move(right)
    move(up)

5. What happens after the loop?

Both indented moves repeat together. Here the knight attempts four moves: right, up, right, up.

An instruction lined up with repeat is outside the loop. It runs after the repetitions finish.

Your turn: write a program that moves right three times, then moves up once. Keep the final move outside the repeat block.

Practice in levels 14–15

  • Do It Again: repeat a simple right-and-up pattern.
  • Repeat, Then Turn: finish a repeated section before making a turn that happens once.

Check your understanding

How many times does the indented move run in repeat(3)?

Three times, unless the level finishes or execution is stopped first.

Does repeating two moves twice mean two moves altogether?

No. It means four moves: the pair is performed twice.

lessons.title: Repeating While Something Is True
lessons.description: Use while to keep repeating an action while a condition is true, instead of choosing a fixed count.
lessons.learning_objective: Explain how while checks before each repetition and use while can(direction) to stop moving when that direction becomes blocked.
lessons.content:
Your puzzle-room goal

A corridor can be one part of a larger puzzle room. Use a while loop to follow it, then continue with the turns or mechanisms needed to reach the exit.

1. What if you do not know the count?

Repeat is useful when you know how many times to act. But sometimes the instruction is “keep going while it is possible.”

For example: while there are dishes left, wash the next dish. After each dish, check again. When none remain, stop.

2. A condition and a loop together

On a straight corridor that ends at a wall, the knight can use:

Try reading this KnightCode program

while can(right):
    move(right)

3. Follow the steps

  1. Check: can the knight move right?
  2. If yes, move right.
  3. Go back and check again.
  4. If no, leave the loop.

If right is blocked at the start, the knight does not run the movement line at all. The condition is checked before moving.

Compare this with if can(right):: if checks once; while keeps checking and repeating.

4. Continue after the loop

Imagine an upward opening at the end of the corridor. After finishing the rightward loop, this program checks the way up:

Try reading this KnightCode program

while can(right):
    move(right)
if can(up):
    move(up)

5. Make sure the loop can finish

A loop should do something that brings it closer to stopping. In this corridor, each move brings the knight closer to the wall. Eventually, moving right is no longer possible.

If the loop keeps checking a blocked direction but its action never changes the situation, it may keep repeating. Ask: “What will eventually make my condition false?”

Your turn: change the first example so the knight keeps moving up while it can.

Practice in levels 16–18

  • Keep Going: use one loop along a straight corridor.
  • Check Again: predict what changes when the knight starts near the end or is already blocked.
  • Stop, Then Turn: finish a loop and continue with a new instruction.

Check your understanding

What is the difference between repeat(3) and while can(right)?

Repeat chooses a fixed count. While keeps checking a condition to decide whether another repetition should happen.

When right becomes blocked, does the while example attempt one more right move?

No. The next check is false, so that movement line is skipped and the loop ends.

lessons.title: Plan, Try, and Improve
lessons.description: Put sequences, decisions, and loops together. Find mistakes by comparing what you expected with what the knight actually did.
lessons.learning_objective: Plan a solution in small parts, use familiar commands together, and explain one correction or improvement after testing.
lessons.content:
Your puzzle-room goal

Your goal is to solve the whole room: reach the exit across the map or open the wall that protects it. Use the commands you know to plan the route and operate its mechanisms.

1. Put your ideas together

You now know three useful ways to guide the knight:

  • Sequence: do instructions in order.
  • Decision: use if and else to choose an action.
  • Repetition: use repeat or while to do something again.

You do not need a new command for every puzzle. Choose which of these ideas helps with each part.

2. Make a small plan

Before typing, describe the route in a few simple parts. For a crate puzzle, your plan might be:

  1. Reach the crate.
  2. Push it onto a plate that accepts crates.
  3. Leave it there and take the open route.

Check each part before combining them. Remember that moving the crate away again may close the door.

3. Read a combined program

Imagine a clear route with two right moves followed by an upward opening. We can repeat the first part and check the next direction:

Try reading this KnightCode program

repeat(2):
    move(right)
if can(up):
    move(up)

4. When the result is different

If the knight does not do what you expected, ask:

  • Did I choose the correct direction?
  • Did I put the instructions in the right order?
  • Are the right lines indented under my if or loop?
  • Did I repeat too many or too few times?
  • Did a door close because its plate was no longer pressed?

Fix one problem, then try again. Finding and fixing a mistake is called debugging.

5. Improve a working solution

First make the solution work. Then look for repeated instructions you can replace with a loop.

Code fuel counts the nonblank lines you submit, including an if or loop header. A loop can use fewer written lines while still making the same number of moves. Shorter code is not automatically a faster route.

After changing the program, run it again to check that it still works. Use the pause-menu restart when you need the whole puzzle returned to its starting setup.

Practice in levels 19–20

  • Find and Fix: correct one mistake in a short crate-and-door plan.
  • Your KnightCode Challenge: plan a route, use the commands you have learned, and explain one choice you made.

Tell your teacher: what did you expect, what happened, and what did you change? Your explanation matters alongside the results of this session.

Check your understanding

Should you shorten the program before you know it works?

Start with a correct solution. Then simplify it and check it again.

Does a mistake mean you have failed to learn programming?

No. Predicting, trying, noticing a difference and correcting it are part of learning to program.

levels.title: First Steps
levels.description: A single straight path. Get the knight to the goal using move() commands in order.

levels.title: Turn the Corner
levels.description: The path bends. Combine directions to follow it around the corner.

levels.title: Tight Corridor
levels.description: A longer, winding path — plan the full sequence before you run it.

levels.title: Check Before Moving
levels.description: Reach the exit across a room divided by a central wall. Plan the route around the wall and use if can() to check a direction before taking that part of the route.

levels.title: What If It Is Blocked?
levels.description: A wall blocks the direct route to the far exit. Let a guarded move be skipped, then guide the knight around the wall through the open passage.

levels.title: You Choose the Condition
levels.description: Navigate two corners and a blocked shortcut to reach the opposite side of the room. Choose conditions that help check your planned route.

levels.title: Right or Up?
levels.description: At a junction around a central obstacle, choose right or up with if/else, then continue to the room’s distant exit. An open direction is not automatically the correct route.

levels.title: When the Answer Is No
levels.description: The preferred passage is blocked, but another route leads around the obstacle to the exit. Use else for the alternative, then finish the room.

levels.title: Is It Blocked?
levels.description: Use blocked() to recognize a blocked passage in a small maze room. Choose the detour and continue through the room to the far exit.

levels.title: Looks Can Be Misleading
levels.description: A wall-looking panel lies on the route to the far side of the room. Test whether it is passable, choose your route, and reach the exit beyond it.

levels.title: Open the Way
levels.description: The exit is behind an openable wall. Reach an ordinary button in a side area, activate it, then return and cross the opened passage to finish the room.

levels.title: Keep It Open
levels.description: A pressure plate controls the wall guarding the exit. Place a crate on the plate, leave it there, and guide the knight along the open route to the other side.

levels.title: Multi-Door Vault
levels.description: Multiple plates and doors in one grid, solved in the right order.

levels.title: Do It Again
levels.description: Cross a room with a repeated right-and-up route. Use repeat() for that pattern, then follow the final passage to the exit.

levels.title: Repeat, Then Turn
levels.description: A repeated corridor leads to a button that opens the exit route. Finish the repetitions, turn once, activate the button, and take the open passage across the room.

levels.title: Keep Going
levels.description: Follow a long corridor inside a puzzle room with while can(). After the loop stops, take the remaining turns to reach the exit on the other side.

levels.title: Check Again
levels.description: Follow a bent route through the room, checking again after each move. Use while loops for its straight sections and continue until the distant exit is reached.

levels.title: Stop, Then Turn
levels.description: The way to the exit goes around a divider and through a button-controlled wall. Combine corridor loops with the button visit and final turn.

levels.title: Find and Fix
levels.description: Fix a plan that reaches a locked wall before the crate holds its plate down. Put the room-solving steps in order, then cross to the exit.

levels.title: Your KnightCode Challenge
levels.description: Solve a complete puzzle room with a repeated approach, a crate-sensitive plate, and an exit behind an openable wall. Plan, test, and explain how your program reaches the goal.
